In ancient India, the wood-worker made war chariots in addition to furniture, doors and panels. The Rigveda mentions him as sutradhar who was also the charioteer of the chariot he made.

No craft has suffered more than wood-carving. Formerly the nobility and well-to-do citizens took delight in embellishing their houses
with carved verandahs and balconies. All the chief entrances were filled with massive carved doors.

It is said to have been introduced in 1764 by Hdfiz Rahmat Khan, who summoned a skilful stone-cutter from Delhi to direct the ornamentation of the Juma Masjid then under construction.
In the hands of his pupils the art was extended to wood, a primary cause being the natural abundance of shisham wood.

The wood par excellence for all kinds of carving is shisham (Dalhergia sissoo), which flourishes universally in the plains as well as on the lower ranges of the Himdlayas. The dark heart-wood is of great durability and is not readily attacked by whiteants.
Cedrela toona or tun is the staple timber of cabinet-makers, notably in the Sahiranpur district. This wood is soft and easily worked, and takes a natural dull-red polish.

The use of unseasonedwood has been the chiefstumbling-block to the adoption of India's lesser known timbers, and the importance of proper seasoning cannot be over-emphasized.
the amount of seasoning which takes place in a log is, to all intents and purposes, negligible, in comparison with the rapid drying which can be effected with converted timber.
experiments have shown that, even after 15 to 20 years, some species have the same amount of moisture in the centre of the log as they had when they were felled.
Water submersion is not a seasoning process, it is merely a method of storage.

there are two important points to be attended to in air-seasoning timber in India.
The proper piling or stacking of the wood.
The protection of the stack from the prevailing hot winds, the blazing Indian sun, and the rain.
Mr. C. V. Sweet, late Seasoning Officer at Dehra Dun, has dealt with this question in detail
He divides the Indian woods into three classes
Woods which are only moderately liable to crack, split, and warp, called medium refractory woods.
Woods which are capable ot withstanding rapid seasoning, or are particularly liable to staining, mould, and decay during seasoning, called non-refractory woods.
Air-seasons easily, and if properly stacked with a good air circulation, it can be dried quickly with little or no depreciation.
Blackwood can be air-seasoned and kiln-seasoned without trouble and with little degrade.

Kiln-seasoning attempts to carry out exactly the same process as natural drying but in a far shorter period of time ; estimated very roughly at one-twelfth of the time required to air-season the same timber.
Kilnseasoning on a small scale is expensive, owing to the large outlay of capital required to instal seasoning kilns.

The preparation of hale wood for lac-turnery begins with seasoning. Logs are cut into small billets and stored away from heat and sunlight in a location with good air circulation for ten days to a month, depending on the moisture content of the wood.
The wood is first seasoned - the planks are stacked and exposed to air, protected from sunlight and rain, for six to seven months.

A peculiarity of the sandal-wood carver of Mysore is that he disdains a file, and does the cleanest and most finished work with the chisel alone, aided by the fine texture of the wood and the extreme sharpness of his tools.
The tools are made from European umbrella spokes, ramrods, and country steel.
A mallet - usually a plain block of wood - and a dozen small chisels will suffice for all purposes.
They fall into two main classes, viz. the flat V chisels known as chaursi; and those with a bent rounded head, used in carving floreated patterns, called hirka.
The lath (adda) consists of two iron bars (killa), one fixed in the oround, the other to be adjusted for distance.
On the inner side of each bar isa spike to which the block of wood to be turned (mochha) is attached.
round which the thong of the bow (kaman) is once passed. The bow is worked backwards and forwards, and thus: imparts the necessary rotatory motion.

Traditionally all lacquerware was produced using simple hand lathes called patris made by local carpenters. A bow string is used to turn a rotating axle in the center of wooden lathe. The turning tool is held in the free hand and pressure is added with the foot, shaping the spinning wood.
The production time decreases considerably on the power lathe as both hands are free to operate turning tools.
Cutting tools are applied to the revolving piece of wood so that thin continuous chips are scraped off.
Once the desired shape is formed, it is sanded with sandpaper while it is still turning, until the surface is smooth and uniform.
the colour is applied by pressing sticks (batti) of coloured lac to the revolving surface.
a stick of sealing-wax (batti) is pressed against it, as it revolves on the lathe. The heat generated melts the lac and thus colours the wood irregularly.
A lac stick of the chosen colour is pressed to the revolving wood. The friction causes the lac to melt and spread uniformly over the area on which it is applied.
The portion of the lac touching the article melts with the heat generated by friction and colours the wood.
An article intended to be ornamented with lac is first turned to the desired shape and polished with a fine powder made from broken pottery. This polishing has the effect of filling up the pores.
Lastly, a cotton rag, dipped in sweet oil (preferably sessanium), is held against the revolving object
the lac takes a polish that it never subsequently loses
the lacquered piece is buffed with the leaves of the talegiri (Pandanus odoratissimus)
Final finishing is done using a screw pine leaf to help spread the lac on the turning wood and polish the object. Buffing lends a translucency to the finished product.

The preparation of lacquer from lac begins with heating and softening.
A specific amount of lithophone is then added to the softened lac and is beaten continuously until a white tint appears.
To prepare the coloured lac sticks, the lac chips are first heated over a coal fire. As they begin melting, dye or colourants are added to the melting lac.
Lacquer pellets are heated slowly in an open oven while the colours and titanium dioxide in powder form are applied to the fluid in small quantity at regular intervals.

The first part of the process of tdrkashi consists of drawing the design in pencil on well-seasoned shisham. The lines are then deeply incised with a sharp knife, and into this brass wire is drawn and beaten down level with the surface of the wood with an iron hammer.
The artisan then lays the wire down on its sharp edge over the groove with one hand, and taps it into place with a hammer held in the other.
The dots that diversify the design and soon run up to thousands in a space of only a few inches square, are minute coils of wire twisted up on the point of a needle.
For the decorative dots, thin wire is coiled around the tip of a needle and often beaten directly into the surface.
The process requires considerable time and labour. A plate of twelve inches diameter will occupy a workman for twenty days.

Thin strips or veneering ribbons are thus made by transverse section on a series of parellel strands and these ribbons are then glued to the surfaces of the boxes, cabinets, etc., as desired.

It may consist of as many as 2,000 separate pieces : these are joined together by a process of dowelling without the assistance of glue, the whole being held together by the frame.
Seed lac is obtained by grinding and washing this stick lac. Shellac is made by melting seedlac or extracting it by a suitable solvent.
It contains, apart from woody matter, the lac resin, lac dye, bodies of insects and some wax.
Lac dye gets its red colour from the laccaic acid present in the hemolymph or body fluid of the lac insect.
It is the colouring matter of the in.sect bodies dead or alive which forms the crimson lac dye when lac is washed. It was for this colouring matter or lac dye, that lac was originally cultivated.

It is obtained by separating the insects from the branch and the resin, crushing them and dissolving the result in an alkaline solution. This solution is then acidified and treated with chalk, which reforms the dissolved dye as a sediment.
